origin_comment: Most inventory systems we evaluated are designed for much larger warehouses. We only need basic receiving and stock counts, but the existing products feel unnecessarily complicated.
We went back to spreadsheets because the inventory software we tried was too expensive for a warehouse with only three employees.
The demo looks polished and the interface is quite clean compared with most warehouse software I have seen.
We eventually built our own spreadsheet template because none of the systems we tested matched the way our small warehouse actually works.
I think inventory software has become much better over the last few years, especially for larger companies.
I built a Python script to clean vendor CSV files and upload the changes automatically. It saves me about two hours every week.
The automation works well until a vendor changes a column name, then I have to spend another hour fixing the script.
Python is surprisingly good for this kind of automation, and the standard library has most of what I usually need.
I have several small scripts running on a cron job because doing these tasks manually every week became too tedious.
It is interesting how many people use Python for small internal tools instead of buying commercial software.
Our company only needs contacts, notes, and follow-up reminders, but most CRMs feel designed for much larger sales teams.
We currently use a shared spreadsheet, and follow-ups are frequently missed because nobody has a clear view of what is overdue.
I have used several CRMs and generally prefer the ones with fewer configuration options.
We stopped using our CRM because adding another user increased the monthly bill more than we expected.
A simple CRM with predictable pricing for small teams is something I would seriously consider paying for.
We reconcile invoices against bank transactions manually at the end of every month, and the process takes about half a day.
Our accounting software handles normal invoices, but unusual supplier formats still require a spreadsheet and manual checking.
The matching algorithm in the demo seems clever and should handle most straightforward cases.
We created spreadsheet formulas to flag mismatches, but they need to be updated whenever suppliers change their invoice format.
The accounting industry has adopted a lot more automation recently, so I expect this problem will become less common.
We use a shared inbox because dedicated helpdesk software feels excessive for a five-person company.
The biggest problem is that two people sometimes answer the same customer while other messages sit unanswered.
I like shared inboxes because everyone can see the conversation history without switching between applications.
We tried a popular helpdesk but abandoned it because configuring all the workflows took longer than managing support manually.
Basic assignment, reminders, and response tracking would probably be enough for our team, and I would prefer that over a complicated helpdesk.
Every Monday I download sales reports from three different services and merge them into a spreadsheet.
The weekly reporting process takes me at least two hours, even though the actual analysis only takes about twenty minutes.
The dashboard in the demo looks much nicer than the spreadsheet we currently use.
I wrote a script to automate part of the reporting process, but an API change broke it last month.
A low-cost reporting service would be interesting if it could connect to our existing payment platforms without requiring a large monthly contract.
Every vendor exports CSV files with slightly different column names, so we clean the files manually before importing them.
I maintain a separate script for each vendor, and every format change creates another maintenance task.
CSV is still one of the most convenient formats for moving structured data between simple business systems.
We have accumulated dozens of small transformation rules over the years because there is no consistent format across our suppliers.
A service that standardized vendor files automatically could remove a surprising amount of repetitive work from our operations team.
We currently coordinate appointments through text messages, and missed appointments cost us real money every month.
Most scheduling tools we evaluated are built around larger teams with complex shift management, which we do not need.
The booking flow in this product is straightforward and much easier to understand than some of the scheduling tools we tested.
We tried an online scheduler but customers found the booking process confusing, so staff went back to handling appointments manually.
We mainly need availability, simple booking, and reminders. Paying for advanced workforce management features would not make sense for us.
Our project management software has dozens of features that nobody on our team uses, and important tasks sometimes get buried under configuration.
We temporarily returned to a simple board and weekly spreadsheet because the full system was slowing down our planning meetings.
The new interface is visually impressive and the animations make the application feel modern.
I would rather pay for fewer features if the software were faster to understand and required less administration.
Project management tools have become a huge category, and there are probably too many products competing for the same customers.
We track recurring operational tasks in a spreadsheet with one row per week, and someone has to copy the checklist forward every Monday.
I made a small script to generate next week's tasks automatically because manually copying the checklist kept getting forgotten.
The recurring task feature looks useful, and I like that the interface does not try to do too much.
The spreadsheet works, but only one person understands all the formulas and nobody else wants to maintain them.
A simple recurring checklist with ownership and reminders would solve most of this without adding much process overhead.
